What an install brings comes from each copy's changelog and files, the repository's settings and its test list. This page changes your installed mods and encodes textures, only when you press a button and, where it matters, confirm.

messages.memory-gotcha-marks: **Marks need this window in front.** Switch here from the game (Alt+Tab), press B, type a few words and press Enter. The moment is taken when you press B, not when you finish typing.
messages.memory-gotcha-restart: **A watch ends when the game closes.** After a restart, start a new one.
messages.memory-gotcha-measure: **Figures are measurements, not a test.** When a watch ends, its report says first what happened (the saves the log shows loaded, your marks): read that before the figures.

Its overview is kept in the tools' cache, outside your repositories, for comparing later.

messages.explorer-gotcha-pause: **Taking a snapshot pauses the game for about half a second.** The game then runs on while the snapshot is read.
messages.explorer-gotcha-held: **A snapshot is let go after ten minutes at most**, when you press Let it go, or when you leave this page. It costs memory while it is held. To look again, take another.
messages.explorer-gotcha-garbage: **A snapshot includes garbage not yet collected**: things nothing holds any more still count until the game's runtime clears them away.

messages.explorer-confirm-question: Take a snapshot of the running game now?
messages.explorer-confirm-words: **Is your game saved?** Taking it pauses the game for about half a second. Nothing in the game is changed: the snapshot is only read. It is let go after ten minutes at most.
messages.explorer-bar-taking: Taking a snapshot of the game…
messages.explorer-take-no-reason: the tools did not say why.
messages.explorer-held-figures: Taken at { $when }. The game paused for { $paused } ms.
messages.explorer-let-go-how: Frees the memory it holds. Key: Q.
messages.explorer-checks-lead: Your repositories' rules for the running game, each asked of this snapshot, so the game is not paused again. A finding is something to look at, not a test: a snapshot holds one moment, and a rule can be wrong.
messages.explorer-released-limit: The snapshot was let go: its ten minutes were up.
messages.explorer-released-ended: The snapshot was let go: the tools reading it stopped early.
messages.explorer-released-gone: The snapshot is no longer held.
messages.explorer-released-left: The snapshot was let go when you left this page.
messages.explorer-gone-object: That thing belonged to a snapshot that has been let go. Every snapshot gives everything a new address, so it cannot be opened again: take another snapshot and find it from the overview.
messages.explorer-gone-kind: That kind was in a snapshot that has been let go. Take another snapshot to look again.
messages.explorer-bar-overview: Reading every object in the snapshot…
messages.explorer-free-how: Free space is room the runtime keeps between objects for new ones. It is not counted in the memory they take.
messages.explorer-garbage-note: A snapshot includes garbage not yet collected: things nothing holds any more still count until the runtime clears them away.
messages.explorer-owners-how: By the file each kind comes from: a mod, the game, or the runtime itself. Biggest first.

messages.explorer-why-title: Why is it still in memory?

messages.ask-tools-local: While it answers, it may ask the tool kit's reports for more facts. Each runs on this computer and is listed below; nothing leaves the computer.
messages.ask-tools-online: While it answers, it may ask the tool kit's reports for more facts. Each runs on this computer first, and you see its answer and choose whether it is sent.

messages.ask-call-declined: { $summary }: you chose not to send it
messages.ask-wait-title: { $service } asks the tool kit for a report
messages.ask-wait-text: It has run on this computer. This is its answer, which goes to the service only if you send it ({ $count } characters):
messages.ask-wait-refused: The tool kit refused it or could not answer. This is what the AI would be told:
messages.ask-tools-unavailable: This model can't use the tool kit's reports, so it answered from what it was sent.
messages.ai-services-tools-title: Let the AI ask the tool kit's reports
messages.ai-services-tools-body: While it answers, the AI may ask the tool kit's read-only reports for more facts, at most six a question: your logs, saves and mods, with home folders as ~. With a model on this computer each runs and is listed. With an online one each runs here first, and you see its answer and choose whether it is sent.
messages.ai-services-tools-kept-on: Kept: the AI may ask the tool kit's reports.
messages.ai-services-tools-kept-off: Kept: the AI answers only from what it is sent.
messages.source-body-chat: An agent you installed yourself (Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI and others), started by the Companion in the repository you choose and talked to through the Agent Client Protocol. Through the Companion it may only read files in that repository and ask your permission; it may change files by itself, as it would in a terminal. Nothing is kept: leaving the page ends it.
messages.chat-reading: Asking the Companion which agent is chosen…
messages.chat-off: The Chat page is switched off, or no agent is chosen. Both are in Settings → AI.
messages.chat-no-repositories: { $game } has no repository on your games list for an agent to work in.
messages.chat-repository-label: The repository the agent works in
messages.chat-warning-own: { $agent } is its own program. It works in { $repository } with your own access to the disk, so it may change or delete files there by itself, as it would in a terminal, and the Companion cannot stop that.
messages.chat-warning-through: Through the Companion it may read files in this repository, each one listed here, and ask your permission for its steps. A change it asks to make through the Companion is shown to you line by line, and made only if you say yes. A command it wants to run is sorted by what it does and handled as Settings → AI says: shown whole and run on your press, run by itself when it only reads or tests (Automatic), or refused; what agents never do here is refused even with a yes.
messages.chat-write-key: Lines marked + are added and lines marked − removed; the rest stay as they are. Nothing is written until you say yes.
messages.chat-not-written: Not changed: { $path }. You said no, and the agent was told.
messages.chat-warning-git: git shows everything that changed. Leaving this page ends the agent, with everything it started.
messages.chat-kit-reports: It can ask the tool kit's reports that read.
messages.chat-no-kit-reports: The tool kit's reports could not be handed to it.
messages.chat-refused-write: It asked the Companion for a file action it does not offer, and was refused.
messages.chat-refused-command: It asked to run a command through the Companion, and was refused: commands are refused in Settings → AI.
messages.chat-stop-refusal: It declined to go on with this.
messages.chat-stop-limit: It reached its limit for one turn.
messages.chat-ended: The agent has ended. Start it again to go on.
messages.chat-panel-body: A Chat page where a whole agent you installed yourself (Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot or Goose) works in a repository you choose, while you talk to it. Each agent uses its own login.
messages.chat-panel-risk: An agent can change or delete files in that repository by itself, at once, so this starts off. Through the Companion it may read, ask your permission, change a file only after you see the change and say yes, and run commands as chosen below.
messages.chat-panel-browser: The Chat page is set up in the desktop program.
messages.chat-panel-kept-on: Kept: the Chat page is on.
messages.chat-panel-kept-off: Kept: the Chat page is off, and any agent running has ended.
messages.chat-panel-shown: Chat is in the page list.
messages.chat-panel-hidden: Chat shows in the page list once it is on and an agent is chosen.
messages.chat-commands-body: How a command the agent wants to run is handled: one it runs with its own tools, once it asks your permission here, and one it asks the Companion to run. Each is sorted first by what it does. A change reaches the next agent you start.
messages.chat-commands-refused-detail: The Companion runs none; its own permission questions come to you
messages.chat-commands-ask-detail: Each shown whole, and run only on your press
messages.chat-commands-automatic-detail: Reading, tests and the tool kit's reports that read run by themselves; the rest asks
messages.chat-commands-kept: Kept: commands are handled as { $mode }. It reaches the next agent you start.
messages.chat-commands-never: In every mode, what agents never do here is refused even with a yes: force-pushing or rewriting git history, skipping the repository's checks, touching your saves, publishing to Steam, reading credentials, changing a repository's visibility, or changing anything outside the repository. The sorting reads a command's words: it is not a sandbox, so only commands that plainly read or test run by themselves.
messages.chat-command-warn: Look twice: this can throw work away, delete, install or stop something.
messages.chat-command-declined: Not run: you said no, and the agent was told.
messages.chat-why-kit-reads: a tool kit report that only reads
messages.chat-why-tests: runs the tests or the checks
messages.chat-why-throws-away-work: can throw away work not yet committed
messages.chat-why-runs-script: runs a script, which can do anything
messages.chat-why-system: changes the computer's own settings or starts other programs
messages.chat-why-unknown: a command the Companion does not know
messages.chat-why-writes-output: writes its output into a file
messages.chat-why-reads-outside: reads outside the repository, or somewhere not named in the text
messages.chat-why-kit-changes: a tool kit command that changes or runs something
messages.chat-why-owner-only: something only you run, on its own page
messages.publish-lead: Each mod's place on the Steam Workshop, its page and the change note Steam will get, and the steps to send it: prepare, upload privately, test it, make it public.
messages.publish-browser: Publishing needs the desktop program: the browser cannot run the tools.
messages.publish-none: No repository of { $game } keeps a Workshop catalogue (config/workshop-publishing.json), so there is nothing to publish here yet.
messages.publish-guide-link: How to set a repository up for publishing
messages.publish-via-steam-how: The Steam client already running and signed in on this PC: nothing is typed and no password is used. It sets the item's tags and Required items too. Steam shows you as playing the game while it sends.
messages.publish-via-steamcmd-how: Valve's SteamCMD, in a window of its own: type your account's password and Steam Guard code there. The Companion never sees them. SteamCMD cannot set tags or Required items, so you set those on the item's page afterwards.
messages.publish-uploads-off: Workshop uploads are switched off in Settings, on the Publishing tab: you can read, edit and prepare, but not upload.
messages.publish-update-all:
{ $count ->
    [one] Update the 1 waiting
   *[other] Update all { $count } waiting
  }
messages.publish-steam-back-off: Read Steam back is off: Workshop pages is switched off under Settings, Going online.
messages.publish-lines:
{ $count ->
    [one] What the tools said (1 line)
   *[other] What the tools said ({ $count } lines)
  }
messages.publish-confirm-update-all:
{ $count ->
    [one] Build, prepare and send the 1 item with a newer version through { $via }?
   *[other] Build, prepare and send all { $count } items with a newer version, dependencies first, through { $via }? It stops at the first that fails.
  }
messages.publish-confirm-create: Upload { $title } { $version } to the Workshop as a new item through { $via }? It starts private: only you can see it until you make it public.
messages.publish-confirm-update: Send { $title } { $version } to item { $item } through { $via }? It stays { $visibility }, and everyone subscribed gets it.
messages.publish-confirm-public: Make { $title } public? Do this only once your private subscription test has passed.
messages.publish-confirm-public-sure: Everyone on Steam will be able to see { $title } { $version } (item { $item }) and subscribe to it, and anyone subscribed gets it at once. Make it public for everyone?
messages.publish-confirm-blockers: Still waiting on: { $blockers }. Only a private upload may go past a hold.
messages.publish-note-covers: What Steam will get with the next upload: { $versions }.
messages.publish-note-omitted: Too long for Steam, so these are named in a closing line instead: { $versions }.
messages.publish-history-none: Nothing has been uploaded from this PC yet.
messages.publish-how: Every check runs before each step. A new item starts private; making it public takes a second, stronger yes. Steam's answer is never taken as proof: open the item and look. Afterwards commit the catalogue, the changelog and any ID file the tools wrote.
messages.publish-prepared: { $mod } is prepared: its release notes are written and a checked candidate is ready to send.
messages.publish-updating-all: Updating every item with a newer version…
messages.publish-updated-all: The updates went to Steam. Open each item and check it, then commit the catalogue.
messages.publish-made-public: { $mod } was sent as public. Open the item and check it, then press Read Steam back to mark the version Released.
messages.publish-uploaded: { $mod } was sent to Steam. Open the item and check it, then commit the catalogue and any ID file.
messages.publish-reading-steam: Reading your items back from Steam…
messages.publish-read-steam: Read back from Steam. Look at what changed in the repository, then commit it.
messages.publish-step-create: Ready for its first, private upload
messages.publish-step-public: Private: make it public after testing
messages.publish-page-saved: Saved. Commit the page with the change it describes.
messages.publish-page-starter: { $path } does not exist yet: this is a starter. Saving writes it.
messages.publish-page-over: Too long: shorten it before saving.

messages.publish-setting-body: Whether the Publish page offers Upload, Make public and Update all waiting. On by default: a new item always starts private, and making one public takes two presses. Off hides those buttons; reading, editing pages and preparing stay.
messages.setup-lead: The Companion brings its own Python and tools. A few pages also use other programs, each needed only by the pages it names. A missing one can be fetched from here: you see the command first, and it runs only when you press Run it.
messages.setup-browser: The setup is read in the desktop program.
messages.setup-reading: Looking for the programs the pages use…
messages.setup-no-games: No games are on your list yet. First steps, on Home, starts it.
messages.setup-group-set-aside: Set aside: you said you don't need these ({ $count })
messages.setup-all-here: Everything the pages use is here.
messages.setup-waits: Needs { $names } first: fetch that, then this.
messages.setup-no-fetcher: The command that fetches it needs { $fetcher }, which isn't on this computer. Use its download page instead.
messages.setup-page-only: Nothing here knows how to fetch it on this system: use its download page.
messages.setup-nothing: It comes with the Companion's installer: installing the Companion again brings it back.
messages.setup-confirm-winget: Windows' own package manager, winget, fetches it from its catalogue and runs its installer. Windows may ask you for an administrator's yes. It can take a few minutes, and the Companion can be used meanwhile.
messages.setup-confirm-dotnet: .NET fetches it from NuGet, Microsoft's catalogue of .NET tools, for you alone. It can take a minute.
messages.setup-running: Running. It can take a few minutes.
messages.setup-stopped: Stopped before it finished. An installer Windows had already started may still finish by itself.
messages.setup-done-not-found: Finished, but { $name } isn't found yet. Press Look again; if it still isn't here, close the Companion and open it again.
messages.setup-failed: It ended with code { $code }, so { $name } may not be installed. What it printed is below.

messages.starters-lead: Most pages need only git and a changelog in a repository; a few read a small file it keeps to opt in. Where one is missing, the Companion can add a starter: you see each file whole first, and it is written only where nothing is, never over a file.
messages.starters-none: No repositories are on your games list yet.
messages.starters-not-found: Its folder isn't there: check it on the Games tab.
messages.starters-no-git: Not kept with git yet: Home, Changes and the Timeline read its history with git, so start it with git first.
messages.starters-all: It has every file the pages read.
messages.starters-add:
{ $count ->

   *[other] Add starter files…
  }
messages.starters-how: Tick the ones you want. Each is written only where nothing is there, and the Companion commits nothing: commit them with git when you're ready.
messages.starters-written: Written into { $repository }. Commit them with git when you're ready.
messages.setup-ai-lead: Nothing here is needed. The Companion can explain things on pages with an AI model, and the Chat page can run an agent in a repository. This finds what is already on your computer: looking and trying happen only when you press.

messages.setup-ai-tried: { $name } answered: it starts and speaks to the Companion.
messages.setup-ai-tried-version: { $name } { $version } answered: it starts and speaks to the Companion.
messages.setup-ai-sign-in: It may ask you to sign in, with: { $ways }.
messages.setup-ai-chat-off: The Chat page is switched off.
messages.ai-programs-body: Let an AI program you already use, such as Claude Desktop, Claude Code, LM Studio or Gemini CLI, ask the tool kit's reports in plain words: why the game logged errors, what is in a save, what changed. You paste the lines below into the program once; it starts the kit's server by itself whenever it needs it.
messages.ai-programs-safe: The program can only ask reports that read. It can never install, publish, change a mod list or run your code, it names a repository only from your games list, and home folders show as ~ in everything it sees. Nothing here goes online.
messages.ai-programs-reading: Asking the tool kit for the lines
messages.ai-programs-browser: The lines come from the tool kit, which only the desktop program can ask.
messages.ai-programs-list-title: Programs that keep a list of servers
messages.ai-programs-list-body: Claude Desktop, LM Studio, Gemini CLI and others. Add this to the program's own list of servers, beside any already there. The program lists it as { $name }.
messages.ai-programs-claude-code-body: Run this once in a terminal. Claude Code then offers the kit's reports in every folder you work in.
messages.ai-programs-copy-failed: That could not be put on the clipboard. Select the lines and copy them instead.
messages.ai-programs-limits: These lines hold this computer's own folders, so they work only on this computer. They have not yet been tried in each program: its own help says where its list of servers lives.
